smm_pool.text: You can now set up custom attribution… Meta announced custom attribution recently as a way to provide different options for how conversions are reported. It’s a shiny object, but I’d reserve this for very limited situations. You need to actually get the volume of results that have helped you determine that custom attribution is useful for you. smm_pool.title: First Impression Ads
smm_pool.text: This could end badly… A few weeks ago, Meta announced the test of a feature in the US called First Impression Ads . This allows advertisers to book the first ad people see in their feeds. Understand that this isn’t some new ad unit that will look any different or a new placement. It’s not new inventory at all. And that could be a problem. Why I’m Concerned This is simply giving advertisers the option to reserve the first ad spot in the feed that was otherwise available to everyone. I worry about the impact this may have. Presumably, this first impression is effective, and it would surely cost more. If it’s not any more effective, then there wouldn’t be a reason to reserve it. If it truly is more effective, it will be in high demand. So let’s assume that the biggest brands then eat up that first impression slot. That removes it from distribution for the rest of advertisers with small and medium-sized budgets. And if that first impression is then rarely available for these other brands, what will it do to results? They’d get worse, right? It all depends on how much results depend on that first impression slot now, and how available that slot becomes when this feature rolls out (assuming it moves beyond a test). Will It Move Beyond a Test? First Impression Ads could be an example of Meta profiting from demand for a select few, while hurting the product for the rest. Or maybe I’m missing something, but it seems like a terrible idea. Stay tuned while we wait to see what happens with this initial test. smm_pool.text: Have you ever had that eerie feeling of entering a room and just knowing people have been talking about you? That happens to your brand every day. People share product recommendations in Instagram Stories, leave feedback in TikTok comments, and (sadly) most of those posts never tag you. So your notifications only show a small part of what people are saying about your brand. That’s where social listening comes in — it shows you what people say about you, your competitors, and your industry when you’re not looking. In this guide, I'll break down what social listening is, how it differs from social monitoring, and how to build your own social listening strategy. Key takeaways Social listening is tracking and analyzing online conversations about your brand, competitors, and industry, including posts that don't tag you, and using what you find to shape your strategy. Social media monitoring tracks what people say to you (tags, mentions, DMs). Social listening looks at what they say about you and why. The main benefits of social listening are deeper audience insight, faster reputation management, earlier trend spotting, better product decisions, and sharper competitive positioning. A workable social listening strategy has five steps: set goals, mine your own comments, pick your keywords, choose tools, and turn the data into decisions.
